packet.headline_seed: Australia politics live: Coalition MPs cross floor in protest against gambling bill; Liberals target Labor on housing crisis in question time
packet.description_seed: Government MPs agree to more than a dozen amendments made with the Coalition. Follow today’s news live Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Chalmers calls gambling amendments ‘very substantial changes’ Treasurer Jim Chalmers says the opt-out register on gambling advertising will be revenue neutral, because the gambling industry will have to cover the costs. These changes that we’re proposing are very substantial changes. And they will make it much easier for people to opt out of this advertising. At the same time, as we make it easier for the regulator to enforce the rules around inducements. I understand people’s concern about inducements. And the minister and the government does as well. I think primarily there’s an important role for the regulator to crack down on and enforce these inducements. There’s absolutely no doubt that the implementation of the reforms has made everything worse for older Australians … the government’s got a lot to do to fix the implementation of these once-in-a-generation reforms that should have and could have and still can be what they were intended to be, but they just aren’t being rolled out like that. If the automation that we’re seeing in aged care is transferred over into the NDIS, yes I have very serious concerns about that. We saw 250,000 older Australians reassessed under aged care. Are we talking over 750,000 Australians who live with disability who possibly need to be reassessed? If they’ve got an algorithm that’s as botched as the one we’ve got in aged care, well we would have very serious concerns and certainly we’ll be raising those matters. Continue reading...

what: Australia politics live: Coalition MPs cross floor in protest against gambling bill; Liberals target Labor on housing crisis in question time

clean_source_blocks.text: Mere weeks ago, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese used the last Question Time before the winter break to pour ice-cold water on the prospect of his government strengthening its gambling legislation. (ABC News: Matt Roberts) Drugs, sex and multi-million dollar high rollers are themes more often featured in a Hollywood film than a parliamentary hearing, but this week's gambling inquiry has been the exception. The explosive evidence heard at the opening of a two-day inquiry into Labor's proposed crackdown on wagering advertising has proved a watershed moment for the increasingly friendless bill. The Greens and crossbenchers have long opposed the federal government's draft, but this week the Coalition also joined the chorus calling for significant changes.

Mere weeks ago, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese used the last Question Time before the winter break to pour ice-cold water on the prospect of his government strengthening its legislation. He implored parliament to pass the reforms, which curtail ads on television and radio at certain times, bans them in stadiums and on player uniforms, and require an online opt-out, but offered a bleak alternative to those who wanted more. "If they don't (vote for the bill), then they do have the option of the status quo," he said. Multiple senior Labor figures have this week referred journalists back to those same words even as the push for stronger measures has grown. They insist that beyond carefully calibrated changes to improve existing measures in the bill, a wholesale rewrite dramatically expanding restrictions is not on Albanese's agenda.

Despite ministers publicly playing down the chances of Labor shelving the bill entirely, that confidence is more borne of the belief that the Coalition will buckle rather than the PM. A sprinkling of Labor MPs have publicly called for the government's bill to go further — longtime advocate Mike Freelander, as well as Louise Miller-Frost and Alicia Payne among them — but even more are making noises privately that inducements must be addressed. (ABC News: David Sciasci) It is unfortunate that Albanese has been on a rare week of leave at the same time the gambling debate has gone from simmering discontent to white-hot anger. If Albanese returns to parliament on Tuesday armed with the same dismissive response to questions about tougher measures, his words will surely prove the match that sets the whole tinderbox alight.
